title: Jumping over the fire

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: What is your favourite holiday tradition? Guess: who in this episode jumped over a fire — Leyla or Sam?

chapters.title: Sam's first Novruz
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 1 SCENE: an evening courtyard in Baku during Novruz, a small bonfire, a red-haired bearded man in a denim shirt jumping over the little fire with a big surprised smile, neighbours clapping, a table with sweets and green wheat sprouts

chapters.title: Old habits die hard
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 2 SCENE: a cosy kitchen, an old grandmother and a young woman with round glasses together making shekerbura pastries with their hands, flour on the table, a warm family moment

chapters.title: Many cultures, one city
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 3 SCENE: a lively international street festival in a modern city, food stalls from different countries, people of many backgrounds dancing in a circle to folk music, colourful lanterns overhead

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is culture and traditions. And I have to tell you about my first Novruz.
[laugh] Oh yes. I was there.
In March my friends in Baku invited me to celebrate. And in the evening, everyone started jumping over small fires!
That's one of our oldest customs. It's a ritual for a new start — you leave the problems of the old year behind.
I was nervous. But my friend said, "When in Rome…" So I jumped too.
And you were great! Only your trousers were in a little danger.
[chuckle] Then there were the sweets — shekerbura, pakhlava. I ate far too many.
That food is part of our heritage. My grandmother makes shekerbura the way her mother did, and her mother before that.
That's lovely. Who taught you?
She did. Every year we make them together. I think every family needs to pass something down — a recipe, a song, a story.
Do you have any superstitions?
[laugh] Some. My grandmother says you mustn't whistle in the house, or money will leave. I don't believe it, but I still never whistle at home.
Old habits die hard!
Exactly. What about your family, Sam?
In England, at Christmas, we pull crackers and wear silly paper crowns. Nobody knows why. It's just what we do.
I think the best cities are multicultural. In Baku you can eat food from twenty countries on one street.
London is the same. But it's important not to lose your own culture. Assimilation is one thing — forgetting where you're from is another.
I agree. My ancestors lived in the mountains, and we still sing their folk songs at weddings.
That's beautiful. I'd love to hear one.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is one tradition from your family that you want to keep — and why?
Mine is the silly paper crown. See you next time!
Bye for now!
